label: International Trade, Investment and Business Law

lessons.title: GATT 1994: The Core Disciplines
body: The World Trade Organization was created by the Marrakesh Agreement, which entered into force on 1 January 1995 as the result of the Uruguay Round. It did not replace the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1947, which had operated since 1948 as a treaty without a formal organization. Instead the WTO absorbed it: the GATT 1994 incorporates the 1947 text and adds understandings, and sits beside separate agreements on services, intellectual property, subsidies, standards and dispute settlement. Joining the WTO is a single undertaking, so a new member accepts the whole package, with limited exceptions for the plurilateral agreements.

Four rules do most of the work in goods trade. First, most-favoured-nation treatment in Article I: any advantage a member gives to a product from one country must be given immediately and unconditionally to the like product from every other member. If Japan lowers its tariff on a type of car from Germany, it must extend the same rate to that car from Korea. Second, tariff bindings in Article II: each member lists maximum tariff rates in its schedule of concessions, and the rate it actually applies may be at or below the bound rate but not above it. Third, national treatment in Article III: once an imported product has cleared the border, internal taxes and regulations must not give it less favourable treatment than a like domestic product. Article III covers internal measures, while tariffs are border measures governed by Article II, which is why a measure's classification matters. Fourth, Article XI generally prohibits quotas, import bans and licensing restrictions, leaving the tariff as the preferred and transparent instrument of protection.

There are important qualifications. Article I allows exceptions for customs unions and free trade areas under Article XXIV, and the Enabling Clause permits preferences for developing countries. Article III has its own carve-outs, including government procurement and certain subsidies to domestic producers. Whether two products are like is decided case by case, with panels and the Appellate Body historically looking at physical properties, end uses, consumer tastes and tariff classification, and, in some reports, the regulatory purpose behind a distinction.

A common trap is to think GATT forbids all discrimination. It forbids discrimination between foreign products from different members (Article I) and between foreign and domestic products (Article III), but it does not stop a member from setting its tariff at any level it has bound, nor from distinguishing between products that are not like each other.

Worked example. State A bound its tariff on imported footwear at 12 percent but applies 8 percent to goods from every member. It then grants a 3 percent rate to footwear from State B only, outside any free trade agreement. This breaches Article I because the better rate must go to like footwear from all members. If instead State A taxes imported footwear at a higher internal sales tax than domestic footwear, the claim is under Article III:2, not Article II.

lessons.title: GATS and TRIPS
body: The General Agreement on Trade in Services covers measures affecting trade in services, defined through four modes of supply. Mode 1 is cross-border supply (a lawyer in London advising a client in Chile by email). Mode 2 is consumption abroad (a patient travelling overseas for surgery). Mode 3 is commercial presence (a foreign bank opening a branch or subsidiary), which is economically the most important. Mode 4 is presence of natural persons (a consultant temporarily sent to work in the host country). Services supplied in the exercise of governmental authority are excluded.

GATS works differently from GATT. Only a few obligations apply across the board, chiefly most-favoured-nation treatment in Article II (subject to a list of exemptions that members registered in 1995) and transparency. The more demanding rules, market access in Article XVI and national treatment in Article XVII, apply only in sectors and modes a member has listed in its schedule, and subject to the limitations it wrote there. This is the positive list or bottom-up approach: a member is bound only where it has said so. Article XVI also names six kinds of prohibited limitations, such as caps on the number of service suppliers or on the value of transactions, unless they are scheduled.

The Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights sets minimum standards that every member must meet, and then leaves members free to choose how to implement them within their own legal systems. It incorporates the substantive rules of the Paris Convention and the Berne Convention (except moral rights), and adds its own: patents must be available in all fields of technology, subject to listed exclusions, and the term of patent protection must last at least 20 years from filing. TRIPS has national treatment (Article 3) and most-favoured-nation treatment (Article 4), the latter being new in international intellectual property law. Unlike the older treaties, it comes with enforcement obligations and access to WTO dispute settlement.

TRIPS includes flexibilities. Article 31 allows compulsory licences with conditions, and the Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health of 2001 confirmed that members may protect public health and set their own grounds for such licences. Because the original Article 31(f) limited compulsory licences to predominantly supply the domestic market, members adopted a waiver in 2003 and then the first-ever amendment to a WTO agreement, Article 31bis, which took effect in January 2017 and lets countries export medicines made under compulsory licence to those without manufacturing capacity.

Worked example. Country X schedules full market access and national treatment for banking in modes 1 and 3 but writes no commitment for legal services. It can restrict foreign law firms from setting up offices without breaching Article XVI or XVII, yet it must still avoid discriminating between foreign law firms from different members unless it listed an MFN exemption.

lessons.title: Dispute Settlement and the Appellate Body Crisis
body: The Dispute Settlement Understanding gives the WTO a compulsory, rules-based system. A member first requests consultations. If they fail, the complainant may ask the Dispute Settlement Body, which is the General Council in another guise, to establish a panel. Under the negative or reverse consensus rule, a panel is established at the second request unless every member, including the complainant, agrees not to. The same rule applies to adopting panel and Appellate Body reports, which removed the veto that a losing party enjoyed under the old GATT. Panels of three experts report to the Dispute Settlement Body; either side can then appeal on issues of law and legal interpretation to the Appellate Body.

The Appellate Body was meant to have seven standing members, serving four-year terms renewable once, and to decide each appeal in about 90 days, with three members per division. Its reports, when adopted, are final. The system's remedy is forward-looking: a member found in breach should bring its measure into conformity within a reasonable period of time. If it does not, the complainant may negotiate compensation or, as a last resort, request authorisation to suspend equivalent concessions (retaliation). Article 23 forbids unilateral determinations of violation, so members must use the system rather than retaliating on their own judgement.

The Appellate Body stopped functioning because the United States, under successive administrations, blocked consensus on filling vacancies, objecting to what it saw as gap-filling and overreach, such as continuing to decide cases past the 90-day limit and treating its own reports as precedent. By 11 December 2019 only one member remained, below the three required to hear an appeal, and the last term expired in November 2020. As of this writing the body has not been restored, despite repeated proposals from a large majority of members and ministerial commitments to reform that did not produce a result.

The consequence is the appeal into the void. A losing party may file an appeal to a body that cannot hear it, and because a report is adopted only after the appeal process concludes, the panel report stays unadopted and unenforceable. To work around this, the EU, China, Canada, Australia and others created the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement, which relies on Article 25 of the DSU (arbitration) to give participants an appeal stage among themselves. It binds only those who join, and the United States and India are not among them.

Worked example. A panel finds that Country P's steel measure breaches GATT Article XI. Country P appeals to the Appellate Body. If both P and the complainant are in the MPIA, an arbitration panel of three appeal arbitrators decides it. If only the complainant is, P's appeal leaves the report unadopted and the complainant cannot seek retaliation through the DSU, though it may negotiate or act under other treaties.

lessons.title: General and Security Exceptions
body: A breach of GATT Article I, III or XI is not the end of the analysis. Article XX allows a member to adopt measures that would otherwise violate GATT if they fall within one of the listed grounds, among them measures necessary to protect public morals (a), to protect human, animal or plant life or health (b), relating to the conservation of exhaustible natural resources if made effective with restrictions on domestic production or consumption (g), and measures necessary to secure compliance with laws not inconsistent with GATT (d). The respondent carries the burden of proof for the exception.

Panels apply a two-tier test. First the measure must fall within a paragraph of Article XX, which typically requires showing that it is necessary (a weighing of the measure's contribution, its trade restrictiveness and the importance of the interest, and a comparison with reasonably available less restrictive alternatives) or related to the objective. Second, the measure must satisfy the chapeau, the opening words, which forbid application in a manner that constitutes arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail, or a disguised restriction on international trade. The chapeau is about how a measure is applied, not its design.

In US - Shrimp (Appellate Body, 1998), the United States banned shrimp caught without turtle excluder devices. The Appellate Body held the measure fell within Article XX(g), since sea turtles are an exhaustible natural resource, but failed the chapeau because the United States negotiated with some countries and not others and applied the certification process rigidly, without regard to local conditions. After the United States revised its approach, a compliance report in 2001 found it satisfied the chapeau. The case shows that environmental measures can survive, if applied in an even-handed way. In EC - Asbestos (2001), the Appellate Body accepted France's ban on asbestos as necessary to protect human life or health under Article XX(b), after finding that health risk was relevant to whether asbestos and substitute fibres were like products.

Article XXI is the security exception. It allows a member to take action it considers necessary for the protection of its essential security interests, in listed circumstances such as war or other emergency in international relations. For decades it was argued that the words it considers made the provision self-judging and beyond review. In Russia - Traffic in Transit (Panel, 2019, WT/DS512), the panel rejected that view: it is for the panel to decide whether the listed circumstances exist objectively, although the member has latitude to define its essential security interests, which must be applied in good faith. Later panels on United States steel and aluminium tariffs (reports circulated in December 2022) followed that reasoning and rejected the security justification. Several members, notably the United States, maintain that Article XXI is self-judging and fully political, and have appealed adverse reports into the void.

Worked example. Country Q bans imports of plastic bags to protect marine life, but exempts bags from two trading partners with whom it has a pending agreement. The ban may fit Article XX(b), but the exemption could fail the chapeau as discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail.

lessons.title: Free Trade Agreements and Customs Unions
body: Regional trade deals are a deliberate exception to the most-favoured-nation rule. GATT Article XXIV permits a customs union or a free trade area if it meets conditions: duties and other restrictive regulations of commerce must be eliminated on substantially all the trade between the parties, and, as to outsiders, the duties and regulations after formation must not on the whole be higher or more restrictive than before. Trade in services has a parallel exception in GATS Article V, which asks for substantial sectoral coverage. Developing countries may also exchange preferences under the Enabling Clause of 1979, which is outside Article XXIV and has looser conditions.

The forms differ in how far integration goes. In a free trade area, members remove tariffs among themselves but each keeps its own external tariff, as in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which entered into force on 1 July 2020 in place of NAFTA. In a customs union, such as the European Union's, members also adopt a common external tariff and a common commercial policy, so goods that enter at one border circulate freely. A common market goes further and adds free movement of services, capital and people, and an economic union coordinates wider policies. Preferential agreements cover far more than tariffs today, with chapters on services, investment, procurement, labour, the environment, digital trade and intellectual property.

Because each free trade area member keeps its own outside tariff, goods could enter through the lowest-tariff member and be shipped on, called trade deflection. Rules of origin prevent this by deciding which goods qualify for preference. Typical tests are that the good is wholly obtained in the region, that its inputs underwent a change in tariff classification, that it reached a regional value content threshold, or that it underwent a specified manufacturing process. The USMCA, for example, adds automotive rules requiring high regional content and a share of production by workers at a stated minimum wage. Origin claims require documentation, and false claims draw penalties and loss of preference.

Turkey - Textiles (Appellate Body, 1999) shows the limits of the defence. Turkey imposed quotas on Indian textile imports when it joined a customs union with the European Communities, arguing that Article XXIV allowed it. The Appellate Body held that the defence is available only if the customs union meets the Article XXIV requirements and the measure was necessary for its formation; Turkey could have formed the union without the quotas, since it could have used rules of origin and other solutions. The USMCA entered into force on 1 July 2020 and includes a joint review at the six-year mark. At the review on 1 July 2026 the United States declined to confirm the 16-year extension, which triggers annual joint reviews; the agreement stays in force on its current terms and, absent an extension, expires on 1 July 2036.

Worked example. Country A, a member of a free trade area, imports yarn from outside the region and weaves it into cloth. The agreement's rule for cloth is a change in tariff heading from yarn. Weaving changes the heading, so the cloth qualifies for the preferential rate when exported to Country B in the same area. If A only dyed imported finished cloth and the rule required a change of heading, the cloth would not qualify.

lessons.title: Tariffs, Classification and Customs Valuation
body: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. It can be ad valorem (a percentage of value), specific (a fixed amount per unit or weight) or compound (both). Duty owed is the product of three questions that every importer faces: what is the good, what is it worth, and where does it come from. Classification, valuation and origin each drive the rate, and each carries penalties for error.

Classification uses the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System, administered by the World Customs Organization, in force since 1988 and revised about every five years. Goods are sorted by a six-digit code that is shared across nearly all countries, and national schedules add further digits (the United States uses the Harmonized Tariff Schedule). The General Rules of Interpretation apply in order: the terms of the headings and any section or chapter notes come first, then rules for mixtures and composite goods, then the heading that appears last in numerical order among equally plausible ones. A set of mixed items is classed by its essential character. Disputes are common, such as whether a device is a toy or a game, or whether a kit is a finished article.

Valuation is governed by the WTO Customs Valuation Agreement, which implements GATT Article VII. The primary method is transaction value, the price actually paid or payable for the goods when sold for export to the importing country, adjusted for specified additions such as commissions, assists supplied by the buyer, royalties that are a condition of sale, and some transport costs, depending on the country's choice. If transaction value cannot be used, for example because the buyer and seller are related and the relationship influenced the price, customs applies fallback methods in a set order: transaction value of identical goods, then similar goods, then deductive and computed value. Undervaluing to cut duty is a common form of customs fraud.

Origin determines the preferential or non-preferential rate and whether trade remedies apply. Non-preferential origin generally follows substantial transformation, the process that gives a product a new name, character or use.

Governments also use tariffs as policy tools outside the negotiated bound rates. In the United States, section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 authorises the President, after a Commerce investigation, to adjust imports that threaten national security, and section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 allows action against foreign practices that are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden United States commerce. In February 2026 the Supreme Court held in Learning Resources v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise tariffs, so tariff measures need a different statutory basis such as section 232, section 301 or the temporary balance-of-payments authority in section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974. Penalties for false customs declarations arise under section 592 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which imposes civil penalties for fraud, gross negligence or negligence, with the level depending on culpability. These measures can raise issues under WTO rules, which is why they are litigated both domestically and before panels.

Worked example. An importer buys 1,000 sets of kitchen knives with a plastic block, paying $20 per set, and the buyer also supplies the supplier with the mould for the block free of charge. The mould's cost, apportioned to these units, is an assist added to transaction value. If the importer declared only $20 per set, it has undervalued the goods and faces liability for the shortfall in duty plus penalties scaled to its level of care.

lessons.title: Technical Barriers, Health Rules and Other Non-Tariff Barriers
body: As tariffs fell, regulatory measures became the main barriers: quotas, licensing schemes, standards, testing and certification, labelling, packaging, local-content rules, procurement preferences and customs formalities. The legal difficulty is that most are legitimate regulation, so the law separates protection of domestic industry from genuine policy aims.

The Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade covers mandatory technical regulations and voluntary standards for products and their processes and production methods where they relate to product characteristics, plus the conformity assessment procedures used to check compliance. Article 2.1 requires national treatment and most-favoured-nation treatment for like products. Article 2.2 requires that regulations not be more trade-restrictive than necessary to fulfil a legitimate objective, taking account of the risks of non-fulfilment, with examples including national security, deception prevention, human health and safety and environmental protection. Article 2.4 requires members to use relevant international standards as a basis for their regulations unless they would be ineffective or inappropriate. In US - Clove Cigarettes (Appellate Body, 2012), the United States banned flavoured cigarettes but excluded menthol ones, which were mostly domestic, and the Appellate Body held that clove and menthol cigarettes were like products and that the difference in treatment was not based on a legitimate regulatory distinction, so it violated Article 2.1. A regulation that disadvantages imports is not automatically a violation, since the detrimental impact must stem from a legitimate regulatory distinction rather than discrimination.

The Agreement on the Application of Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures governs food safety and animal and plant health measures. It lets members set their own level of protection, including a high one, but demands that measures be applied only to the extent necessary, be based on scientific principles, and not be maintained without sufficient scientific evidence. Article 3 encourages measures based on international standards (such as those of the Codex Alimentarius Commission), and Article 5 requires measures to rest on a risk assessment suited to the circumstances. Article 5.7 permits provisional measures when relevant evidence is insufficient, if the member seeks more information and reviews within a reasonable time. In EC - Hormones (Appellate Body, 1998), the European Communities banned beef from cattle treated with certain growth hormones. The Appellate Body held that the ban was not based on a risk assessment as Article 5.1 requires, because the evidence presented did not support the measure, while rejecting a narrow view of what counts as science, since a risk assessment can reflect divergent views of qualified experts.

Other barriers have separate rules. Import licensing is disciplined by the Agreement on Import Licensing Procedures, local-content requirements by the Agreement on Trade-Related Investment Measures and GATT Article III:4, and quantitative restrictions by Article XI. Government procurement is largely outside the core rules but is covered by the plurilateral Agreement on Government Procurement for its parties.

Worked example. Country Z requires all imported toys to pass testing in a laboratory located in Z, but accepts domestic toys on the manufacturer's own declaration. This sets a different conformity assessment burden for imports, so a TBT claim would focus on Articles 2.1 and 5, asking whether the difference is justified by a legitimate objective or only protects domestic producers.

lessons.title: Trade Remedies: Anti-Dumping, Subsidies and Safeguards
body: Trade remedies let a member raise duties above its bindings in specific, regulated circumstances. Three exist: anti-dumping duties against dumped imports, countervailing duties against subsidised imports, and safeguards against surges in fairly traded imports. The first two respond to what is treated as unfair trade, while safeguards respond to injury alone, and the conditions differ accordingly.

Dumping occurs when a product is exported at less than its normal value, usually the price in the exporter's home market, or if that is unavailable or unrepresentative, a price to a third country or a constructed value of cost plus profit. The Anti-Dumping Agreement allows duties only if three things are shown: dumping, material injury (or threat of it, or material retardation of an industry) to the domestic industry, and a causal link between them. The duty may not exceed the dumping margin. Some members, such as the European Union, apply a lesser duty rule, charging only what is needed to remove the injury, but the Agreement makes this optional and the United States does not use it. Measures lapse after five years unless a sunset review finds that expiry would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping and injury. The method of zeroing, which treats sales above normal value as zero when averaging, has been repeatedly found inconsistent with the Agreement in many disputes, yet remains contested.

The Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures defines a subsidy as a financial contribution by a government or public body that confers a benefit, and then applies its rules only to specific subsidies, those targeted at an enterprise, industry or region. Prohibited subsidies are those contingent on export performance or on using domestic over imported goods. Actionable subsidies are not banned but can be challenged at the WTO if they cause adverse effects to another member's interests, or be offset by countervailing duties if they injure a domestic industry. Domestic industry must be injured and the duty may not exceed the subsidy's amount.

Safeguards, under GATT Article XIX and the Agreement on Safeguards, apply when increased imports, in absolute or relative terms, cause or threaten serious injury, a higher standard than material injury. Safeguards must be applied to all sources on a most-favoured-nation basis, may last four years with extension to a maximum of eight, and must be progressively liberalised if longer than a year. Affected exporters may obtain compensation or, after three years in some cases, retaliate. Because they do not require any wrongdoing, safeguards are used less than anti-dumping duties.

In the United States, Title VII of the Tariff Act of 1930 divides roles: the Department of Commerce determines the margin of dumping or subsidy, and the International Trade Commission determines injury. Both must be affirmative for duties to issue.

Worked example. A domestic steelmaker complains that Country M's exporter sells at 30 percent below its home price and that its own sales and employment fell as the imports rose. The authority finds a 22 percent margin and material injury, and imposes a duty of 22 percent or, under a lesser duty rule, perhaps 15 percent if that removes the injury. If the imports were fairly priced but surging, only a safeguard could be used, and it would have to apply to all suppliers.

lessons.title: The CISG: Scope and Contract Formation
body: The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods, concluded in Vienna in 1980 and in force since 1 January 1988, is the most successful uniform commercial treaty. It has been adopted by a large majority of the world's major trading nations, including the United States, China, Germany, France, Japan and Australia, though not the United Kingdom or India as of this writing. In a state that is a party, the CISG is the domestic law for qualifying international sales, so it is not merely a model.

The Convention applies to contracts of sale of goods between parties whose places of business are in different states, when either both states are contracting states (Article 1(1)(a)) or the rules of private international law lead to the law of a contracting state (Article 1(1)(b)). The United States, China and a few others declared a reservation under Article 95 against paragraph (1)(b), so a US court applies the CISG only when both states are parties. Article 2 excludes sales of goods bought for personal, family or household use, auctions, securities, ships and aircraft, and electricity. Article 3 treats contracts for goods to be manufactured as sales unless the buyer supplies a substantial part of the materials, and excludes contracts where the preponderant part is labour or services. The CISG does not govern the validity of the contract or the effect on property in the goods (Article 4) or liability for personal injury caused by the goods (Article 5), so those questions fall to domestic law.

Parties can exclude the CISG or vary its terms (Article 6), but a clause choosing the law of a contracting state, such as New York or German law, does not exclude it, because the CISG is part of that law. To opt out, the contract should say that the CISG does not apply. Gaps are filled by the Convention's general principles, and only if none exists by the law that private international law designates (Article 7(2)).

Formation differs from common law in several ways. No writing is required unless a state has made a reservation (Articles 11 and 96). An offer must be sufficiently definite, naming goods and expressly or implicitly fixing or providing a way of determining quantity and price (Article 14). An offer may be revoked until the offeree sends an acceptance, unless it states a fixed time or is otherwise irrevocable, including through reasonable reliance (Article 16), so there is no consideration doctrine and no need for an option payment. Acceptance takes effect when the assent reaches the offeror, not when it is sent, so the common law mailbox rule does not apply (Article 18(2)), and silence is not acceptance. A reply with additional terms that do not materially alter the offer is an acceptance unless the offeror objects promptly, whereas a reply that changes price, payment, quality, quantity, delivery, extent of liability or dispute resolution is a counter-offer (Article 19). This reduces the mirror-image problem, though the battle of the forms still generates disputes.

In MCC-Marble (11th Cir. 1998), the court held that the parol evidence rule does not apply under the CISG, since Article 8 directs courts to consider all relevant circumstances, including negotiations, in interpreting a party's statements.

Worked example. A seller in Ohio offers machinery to a buyer in Germany for a fixed price, and the buyer replies that it accepts but asks for a longer warranty period. Both states are parties and no one opted out, so the CISG applies. A warranty change affects the extent of liability, which is a material alteration under Article 19(3), so the reply is a counter-offer and there is no contract until the seller assents.

lessons.title: The CISG: Performance, Breach and Remedies, and Incoterms
body: The CISG sets a single regime for breach, whatever the type of obligation. The seller must deliver goods that conform to the contract in quantity, quality and description, and, unless the parties agree otherwise, goods fit for the purposes for which goods of that kind are ordinarily used and fit for any particular purpose expressly or impliedly made known to the seller (Article 35). The buyer must examine the goods within as short a period as is practicable (Article 38) and give notice of a lack of conformity, specifying its nature, within a reasonable time after discovering it or when it ought to have discovered it, and in any case within two years of handing over (Article 39). A buyer who fails to give timely notice loses the right to rely on the defect, which is a frequent trap in litigation.

Remedies depend on the seriousness of the breach. A fundamental breach (Article 25) is one that results in such detriment as substantially to deprive the other party of what it is entitled to expect under the contract, unless the breaching party did not foresee, and a reasonable person in the same circumstances would not have foreseen, that result. Only a fundamental breach lets the buyer declare the contract avoided (Article 49) and the seller likewise (Article 64). For lesser breaches the buyer can require performance, repair or substitute goods (Article 46), reduce the price (Article 50), or fix an additional period for performance (Article 47), which, if the seller does not meet it, can support avoidance for non-delivery. Courts need not order specific performance unless their own law would do so for similar contracts (Article 28).

Damages under Article 74 equal the loss, including lost profit, suffered by the other party as a consequence of the breach, but may not exceed the loss the breaching party foresaw or ought to have foreseen at the time of contracting. A party relying on a breach must take reasonable steps to mitigate (Article 77), and may recover interest (Article 78). A party is excused for failure caused by an impediment beyond its control that it could not reasonably have been expected to take into account or avoid (Article 79). In Delchi Carrier v. Rotorex (2d Cir. 1995), a buyer received compressors that failed to meet the specified cooling capacity, and the court held that this was a fundamental breach and awarded lost profits and incidental damages under Article 74.

The CISG says little about the practicalities of delivery, so merchants use Incoterms, rules published by the International Chamber of Commerce, now in the 2020 edition. They are not law. They apply only if incorporated into the contract, and they define who arranges and pays for transport, when risk passes and who handles export and import clearance. There are eleven rules, such as EXW (ex works), FCA (free carrier), CPT and CIP (carriage paid), DAP (delivered at place), DPU (delivered at place unloaded) and DDP (delivered duty paid), plus the sea-only rules FAS, FOB, CFR and CIF. Under FOB the seller delivers when the goods are loaded on the ship at the named port, and the buyer bears risk and costs from that point. Under CIF the seller pays freight and a minimum level of insurance to the destination port, yet risk still passes on loading. Incoterms deal with delivery, costs and risk, not with title or payment.

Worked example. A buyer in Spain receives machinery from a seller in Canada on CIF Barcelona terms. The ship sinks in transit after leaving port. Risk passed to the buyer on loading, so the buyer must still pay the price, and its remedy is the insurance the seller was required to arrange.

lessons.title: International Commercial Arbitration: Agreement, Seat and Procedure
body: International commercial arbitration is the default method for resolving cross-border commercial disputes. The reasons are mainly practical. A court judgment obtained in one country is difficult to enforce in another, while an arbitral award is enforceable in a large number of states under a single treaty. Arbitration gives parties a neutral forum, a choice of decision-makers with expertise, flexible procedure, confidentiality in many systems (though not guaranteed everywhere), and a final award with narrow grounds for challenge. Disadvantages include cost, limited joinder of third parties, little power over non-parties, and no appeal on the merits.

Arbitration rests on consent, expressed in an arbitration clause or a submission agreement. Four features of the clause matter. First, separability: the clause is treated as a separate agreement from the main contract, so a claim that the contract is invalid does not by itself defeat the clause. The US Supreme Court applied this under the Federal Arbitration Act in Prima Paint v. Flood and Conklin (1967) and Buckeye Check Cashing v. Cardegna (2006), and the UNCITRAL Model Law adopts it in Article 16. Second, competence-competence: the tribunal can rule on its own jurisdiction. Third, the seat, the legal place of arbitration, which determines the procedural law (lex arbitri) and the courts that supervise the arbitration and hear applications to set aside the award; it need not be where hearings are physically held. Fourth, the governing law of the contract, which can differ from the law of the seat and the law of the arbitration agreement. Tribunals usually apply the law the parties chose.

The parties choose between ad hoc arbitration, often under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, and institutional arbitration under rules of bodies such as the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), the London Court of International Arbitration, the Singapore International Arbitration Centre, the Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre or the International Centre for Dispute Resolution. Institutions administer the case, appoint arbitrators if the parties cannot, and some scrutinise draft awards (the ICC does). The UNCITRAL Model Law of 1985, amended in 2006, has been the basis for the arbitration statutes of many jurisdictions and sets out the extent of court intervention. Many modern rules provide for emergency arbitrators for urgent relief before the tribunal is formed. The International Bar Association's rules on evidence and its guidelines on conflicts of interest are soft law that tribunals often follow when the parties adopt them or the tribunal finds them useful.

The question of who decides whether a dispute is arbitrable arises often. In First Options v. Kaplan (US 1995), the Supreme Court held that, in the United States, courts decide arbitrability independently unless the parties clearly and unmistakably agreed that the arbitrator would decide it. Delegation clauses and incorporation of institutional rules are often relied on as that agreement.

Worked example. A supply contract between a Korean firm and a Brazilian firm says disputes will be arbitrated in Singapore under SIAC rules and governed by Swiss law. The Korean firm later claims the contract was procured by fraud. Because of separability, the tribunal can hear the dispute, deciding under Swiss law, while Singapore courts supervise the arbitration and any set-aside application.

lessons.title: The New York Convention: Recognition and Enforcement
body: The Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, concluded in New York in 1958 and in force since 1959, has more than 170 parties, including nearly all major trading nations, and is the keystone of international arbitration. It does two jobs. Under Article II, a court of a contracting state seized of a matter covered by a written arbitration agreement must refer the parties to arbitration, unless the agreement is null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed. Under Articles III and IV, each state must recognise awards as binding and enforce them under its own procedural rules, without imposing substantially more onerous conditions than for domestic awards, on the application of the party relying on the award, which supplies the original or a certified copy of the award and of the agreement.

The Convention applies to awards made in a state other than the one where recognition is sought, and to awards not considered domestic where enforcement is sought (Article I). A state may declare two reservations: reciprocity, limiting application to awards made in another contracting state, and commercial, limiting it to disputes considered commercial under national law. The United States made both.

Refusal is limited to the exhaustive list in Article V. On the request of the party resisting enforcement, who bears the burden, the court may refuse if: (a) a party lacked capacity or the agreement was invalid under the applicable law; (b) the resisting party was not given proper notice or was otherwise unable to present its case; (c) the award deals with matters beyond the scope of the submission; (d) the tribunal's composition or procedure was not in accordance with the agreement or the law of the seat; or (e) the award is not yet binding or has been set aside or suspended by a competent authority in the country where it was made or under whose law it was made. On its own motion, the court may refuse if the subject matter is not capable of settlement by arbitration under its law, or if recognition would be contrary to its public policy (Article V(2)). The word may matters, since courts retain some discretion even where a ground is established, and courts generally read the grounds narrowly, so enforcement refusals are uncommon. Public policy is usually understood as international public policy or the most basic notions of morality and justice, rather than any rule of local law. Article VI permits a court to adjourn enforcement while a set-aside application is pending, and Article VII lets a party rely on a more favourable national law or treaty.

The US Supreme Court has been supportive. In Scherk v. Alberto-Culver (1974) it enforced an international arbitration clause even though securities claims might not have been arbitrable domestically, stressing the need for predictability in international deals. In Mitsubishi Motors v. Soler (1985) it held that statutory antitrust claims arising from an international transaction can be arbitrated under the Convention.

Worked example. A Dutch company obtains an ICC award in Paris against a Texan firm, which has no assets in France. The Dutch company asks a Texas federal court to confirm the award. The Texan firm argues that the tribunal misapplied the law, but error of law is not an Article V ground, so the court cannot review the merits and will confirm unless a listed ground, such as lack of notice, is proved.

lessons.title: Investment Treaties and Investor-State Arbitration
body: Foreign investors hold assets in a state they do not control, so they fear expropriation, discrimination and arbitrary treatment, and host governments want capital. Thousands of bilateral investment treaties and investment chapters in trade agreements respond by giving covered investors substantive protections and a right to bring claims directly against the host state before international arbitrators, bypassing the host state's courts. This is investor-state dispute settlement.

The usual protections are these. Expropriation, direct or indirect, is allowed only for a public purpose, without discrimination, by due process and with prompt, adequate and effective compensation. Indirect expropriation covers measures that, without taking title, substantially deprive the investor of the value of the investment, and tribunals ask about the measure's economic impact, its interference with reasonable expectations, and its character, including whether it is a bona fide regulation for a public purpose. Fair and equitable treatment is the most invoked standard and is often read to cover denial of justice, arbitrary or discriminatory conduct, breach of legitimate expectations created by specific assurances, and lack of due process; treaties differ on whether it equals the minimum standard of treatment under customary international law. Others include full protection and security, national treatment and most-favoured-nation treatment, free transfer of funds, and sometimes an umbrella clause that elevates contract commitments to treaty obligations.

The best-known forum is the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, created by the Convention of 1965 (the Washington Convention) and part of the World Bank Group. Article 25 requires a legal dispute arising directly out of an investment between a contracting state and a national of another contracting state, with written consent. Awards are final and not subject to appeal or national court review (Article 53); the only internal check is annulment by an ad hoc committee under Article 52 on narrow grounds, such as manifest excess of powers, serious departure from a fundamental rule of procedure, or failure to state reasons. Each contracting state must recognise the pecuniary obligations in an award as if it were a final judgment of its own court (Article 54), though immunity from execution against state assets is preserved (Article 55). Claims can also proceed under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules or the ICSID Additional Facility, in which case ordinary arbitration law at the seat applies, including set-aside.

Cases illustrate the tension between investor protection and regulation. In Metalclad v. Mexico (2000), a tribunal found that a municipality's denial of a construction permit for a hazardous-waste facility, after federal officials gave assurances it was not needed, amounted to expropriation and unfair treatment under NAFTA. In Methanex v. United States (2005), a tribunal rejected a claim against California's ban on a gasoline additive, finding that a non-discriminatory regulation for a public purpose, adopted with due process, is ordinarily not expropriation unless the state gave specific commitments to refrain from it.

Worked example. A mining company with a licence and assurances from the ministry invests heavily, and the state then revokes the licence without a hearing, citing a vague environmental concern, and awards the site to a local firm. The investor can argue indirect expropriation, denial of due process under fair and equitable treatment and discrimination, and can seek compensation from a tribunal if the applicable treaty offers consent and the company qualifies as a protected investor.

lessons.title: The ISDS Debate and Reform
body: Investor-state arbitration is among the most disputed parts of international economic law, and good analysis starts with the strongest version of each side. Supporters argue that it depoliticises investment disputes by replacing diplomatic pressure with neutral law, gives investors a remedy where local courts are biased, slow or captured, and thereby helps attract investment and encourages good governance. They point out that treaty standards bind only against arbitrary or discriminatory conduct and that states mostly win or settle claims. Critics reply that it gives foreign investors a privileged route unavailable to domestic firms or citizens, can chill legitimate regulation on health, environment and finance through the threat of large claims, lacks an appeal and a system of precedent so that similar treaty language yields inconsistent outcomes, relies on arbitrators who may also act as counsel, and is costly. Empirical work on whether treaties increase investment flows is mixed, so neither side can claim the evidence settles the matter.

The current legal position is a patchwork. In Slovak Republic v. Achmea (Court of Justice of the European Union, 2018), the court held that an arbitration clause in a bilateral investment treaty between two EU member states is incompatible with EU law because it removes disputes from the courts of member states that apply EU law. In Komstroy (2021), the court extended the reasoning to intra-EU claims under the Energy Charter Treaty. Member states agreed in 2020 to terminate their intra-EU investment treaties, though arbitral tribunals and some courts outside the EU have not always accepted that the EU-law objection prevents them from hearing claims under the Energy Charter Treaty or the ICSID Convention, and enforcement of such awards in non-EU courts remains contested. Several states have withdrawn from the Energy Charter Treaty in the wake of its modernisation talks, and the European Union and Euratom withdrawal took effect on 28 June 2025, although 17 EU member states remain parties.

Tribunals also police abuse. In Philip Morris Asia v. Australia (2015), a tribunal under a Hong Kong-Australia treaty declined jurisdiction because the company had restructured to gain treaty protection when a dispute over plain-packaging laws was already foreseeable, which it regarded as an abuse of rights. The case shows that treaty shopping is acceptable in principle, since structuring in advance is lawful, but not after the dispute is reasonably foreseeable.

Treaty design changes in response. The USMCA ended investor-state arbitration between the United States and Canada and kept it for Mexico and the United States only for specified sectors and for legacy claims during a transition. The EU's agreements propose a standing investment court with an appeal tribunal. At UNCITRAL, a working group has worked on reform proposals such as a standing mechanism, an appellate body and an advisory centre, though no consensus on a single system has emerged. The ICSID Rules were amended with effect from July 2022 to cover transparency, third-party funding disclosure and expedited procedures.

Worked example. A Dutch holding company acquires a subsidiary in State X after X announces a new tax and a public dispute with the original owner arises. The company then files a claim under the Netherlands-X treaty. A tribunal may decline jurisdiction because the dispute was foreseeable when the restructuring occurred, applying the abuse-of-process reasoning in Philip Morris, though not all tribunals draw the line identically.

lessons.title: Sanctions and Export Controls
body: Sanctions and export controls are foreign policy tools that operate through private companies. Sanctions restrict dealings with particular countries, entities or individuals, while export controls restrict the transfer of goods, software and technology that have military or other sensitive uses. For a business, the practical result is that a deal can be lawful under contract and trade law and still be prohibited.

In the United States, most sanctions rest on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, under which the President, after declaring a national emergency, can block property and prohibit transactions. The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control administers programmes and publishes the Specially Designated Nationals list. Designated persons' property in United States jurisdiction is blocked, and US persons, which includes citizens, residents, entities organised under US law, their foreign branches and anyone in the United States, generally may not deal with them. Under OFAC's 50 percent rule, an entity owned 50 percent or more in the aggregate, directly or indirectly, by blocked persons is itself blocked even if not listed. Civil liability is strict: no intent is needed, though knowledge and willfulness affect penalties and criminal exposure. Secondary sanctions threaten non-US parties who deal with targets, by cutting them off from the US financial system or listing them. Non-US banks have paid very large settlements for processing dollar payments for sanctioned parties, as in BNP Paribas's 2014 guilty plea and payment of about 8.9 billion dollars.

Other systems operate in parallel. UN Security Council sanctions under Chapter VII, Article 41 of the Charter bind all members under Article 25 and are implemented through national law. The European Union adopts restrictive measures through a unanimous Council decision under its common foreign and security policy and then a regulation under Article 215 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which is directly applicable to EU persons and business in the EU. Because rules differ, multinational firms face conflicts; the EU's Blocking Regulation, for example, prohibits compliance by EU operators with certain US extraterritorial measures on Cuba and Iran.

US export controls come in two main systems. The Export Administration Regulations, issued under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 and administered by the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, control dual-use items listed on the Commerce Control List by export control classification number, and the Entity List adds licence requirements for named foreign parties. The regulations reach re-exports and, through the foreign direct product rule, some foreign-made goods derived from US technology, and treat release of controlled technology to a foreign national in the United States as a deemed export. The International Traffic in Arms Regulations, issued under the Arms Export Control Act and administered by the State Department, control items on the US Munitions List. The Wassenaar Arrangement is a voluntary multilateral coordination body for conventional arms and dual-use goods, not a treaty with binding force.

Worked example. A US software firm sells licences to a distributor in Dubai. The distributor is 60 percent owned by a company on the SDN list. Although the distributor is not itself listed, the 50 percent rule makes it blocked, so the firm should not deal with it. The firm needs screening of owners, contractual sanctions clauses and a licence analysis for its encryption software.

lessons.title: Anti-Corruption and Foreign Investment Screening
body: Two further regimes shape cross-border deals. The first is anti-corruption law, which prohibits paying officials to win business. The second is foreign investment screening, which lets governments block or condition inbound deals on security grounds.

The United States Foreign Corrupt Practices Act of 1977 has two parts. The anti-bribery provisions prohibit offering or giving anything of value corruptly to a foreign official, a party official or a candidate, to influence an act or decision or secure an improper advantage in order to obtain or retain business. They apply to issuers of US-listed securities, domestic concerns, and persons who act in furtherance while in US territory, and companies are liable for agents and intermediaries when they know of the payment, with knowledge including awareness of a high probability, so willful blindness is not a defence. There is an exception for facilitating payments for routine governmental action, and affirmative defences for payments lawful under the written laws of the foreign country and for reasonable bona fide promotional or contractual expenses. The accounting provisions require issuers to keep accurate books and records and maintain adequate internal controls, and they apply even where no bribe is proved. The Justice Department enforces the criminal provisions and the Securities and Exchange Commission handles civil enforcement against issuers. Enforcement priorities have shifted in recent years, including a pause and revised guidelines in 2025, so the current policy should be checked.

Other systems differ. The OECD Anti-Bribery Convention of 1997 obliges parties to criminalise bribery of foreign public officials. The United Nations Convention against Corruption of 2003 is broader, covering domestic bribery, asset recovery and prevention. The UK Bribery Act 2010 criminalises both giving and receiving bribes, covers private-sector bribery, has no exception for facilitation payments, and creates a corporate offence in section 7 of failing to prevent bribery by an associated person, with a defence for having adequate procedures. A multinational therefore usually builds its policy on the strictest regime that reaches it, with due diligence on intermediaries, contractual anti-corruption clauses, audit rights and training.

Foreign investment screening applies national security review. In the United States, the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, established under the Exon-Florio provision of 1988 and expanded by the Foreign Investment and National Security Act of 2007 and the Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act of 2018, reviews transactions that could result in foreign control of a US business, as well as certain non-controlling investments in businesses dealing with critical technology, critical infrastructure or sensitive personal data, and certain real estate deals. Some filings are mandatory, and the President may block or unwind a transaction. The European Union's 2019 regulation (2019/452) created a cooperation mechanism among member states, which keep their own screening laws; Regulation (EU) 2026/1386 will replace it from 17 January 2028 and make national screening mandatory across a minimum set of sectors, and the United Kingdom's National Security and Investment Act 2021 introduced a mandatory notification regime for acquisitions in sensitive sectors.

Worked example. A US-listed company hires a local agent in a country where customs clearance is slow, paying a large success fee, and part of the fee is passed to a customs officer. The company's staff saw red flags but did not ask. Under the FCPA, the company can be liable for the bribe through the agent because it was aware of a high probability, and its books recording the fee as consulting violate the accounting provisions.

lessons.title: Cross-Border Data Flows and Privacy Rules
body: Data is now a traded input, and rules about personal data increasingly decide where and how a business can operate. The leading model is the EU's General Data Protection Regulation, in application since May 2018. It applies to organisations established in the EU and, under Article 3(2), to organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour there. Violations can bring fines of up to 4 percent of worldwide annual turnover or 20 million euros, whichever is higher, for the most serious infringements (Article 83).

Chapter V restricts transfers of personal data outside the EU unless the level of protection is not undermined. There are three main routes. An adequacy decision under Article 45 is a finding by the European Commission that a country, territory or sector ensures an essentially equivalent level of protection, after which data flows freely. Absent adequacy, a transfer needs appropriate safeguards under Article 46, most commonly standard contractual clauses approved by the Commission (a new set was adopted in 2021) or binding corporate rules for intra-group transfers (Article 47). Finally, narrow derogations in Article 49, such as explicit consent for a specific transfer, are interpreted strictly and not for routine flows.

The Court of Justice has policed the system. In Schrems I (2015), the court invalidated the Safe Harbour adequacy decision for transfers to the United States, because United States law allowed public authorities access to the data without adequate limits or redress. In Schrems II (2020), the court invalidated the successor Privacy Shield decision on similar grounds, relating to surveillance programmes and the lack of effective remedies for EU persons, but upheld standard contractual clauses in principle, requiring exporters and importers to check case by case whether the law of the destination country allows the clauses to be honoured and, if not, to add supplementary measures or suspend the transfer. After United States Executive Order 14086 of 2022 set new limits on signals intelligence and created a Data Protection Review Court, the Commission adopted an adequacy decision for the EU-US Data Privacy Framework in July 2023, covering certified US companies. The General Court dismissed one challenge (Latombe v Commission, T-553/23) on 3 September 2025; the applicant appealed to the Court of Justice on 31 October 2025 (C-703/25 P), and that appeal was pending as of October 2026 on the sources checked, so the framework's durability should be checked as of any given date.

Other jurisdictions take different paths. China's Personal Information Protection Law (effective November 2021) and Data Security Law, together with the Cybersecurity Law, require security assessments, standard contracts or certification for exports of personal information above thresholds and for important data. Several countries require local storage of certain data. The United States has no comprehensive federal privacy statute but has sector laws and state laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act; its Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act of 2018 lets US authorities compel US-based providers to produce data held abroad, which can conflict with foreign rules. Trade agreements now regulate data directly: the USMCA and the CPTPP require parties to allow cross-border transfers and bar data localisation, subject to legitimate public policy exceptions that cannot be applied as arbitrary discrimination or disguised restrictions on trade.

Worked example. A US software provider with EU customers hosts their customer data in US data centres. It should check whether it is covered by an adequacy decision (for example through certification under the Data Privacy Framework) or else execute standard contractual clauses with a transfer impact assessment, and consider whether any local-storage rule in another market adds a separate constraint.

lessons.title: International Intellectual Property Treaties
body: Intellectual property rights are territorial: a US patent is enforceable only in the United States, and a French copyright is a right under French law. International treaties do not create global rights. They do three things instead: oblige states to give foreigners the same protection as nationals, set minimum standards, and simplify the procedures for obtaining rights in many countries.

The Paris Convention of 1883 governs industrial property, including patents, trademarks and designs. Its core rules are national treatment, the right of priority and the independence of patents. Priority lets an applicant who files in one member state claim that filing date in others if they file within 12 months for patents and utility models, or six months for designs and trademarks. Independence means a patent in one country is separate from patents on the same invention elsewhere, so the grant, refusal or invalidation in one has no automatic effect in the others.

The Berne Convention of 1886 governs copyright. It also rests on national treatment, and adds that protection is automatic, without registration or other formalities, and independent of protection in the country of origin. It sets minimum rights, including authors' moral rights (Article 6bis) and a minimum term of life of the author plus 50 years (Article 7), though many states give life plus 70. TRIPS incorporates the substantive Berne rules, other than moral rights, making them enforceable through the WTO, and the WIPO Copyright Treaty of 1996 adds protection for computer programs and databases and obligations on technological protection measures.

Two registration systems reduce cost. The Patent Cooperation Treaty of 1970 lets an applicant file one international application, receive an international search report and a non-binding opinion, and then enter the national or regional phase, typically 30 months from the priority date. It does not grant an international patent: each national office decides patentability under its own law. The Madrid System, under the Madrid Agreement of 1891 and the Madrid Protocol of 1989, lets a trademark owner extend a home registration or application to many designated countries through one filing, but the international registration depends on the basic mark for its first five years, so cancellation of the basic mark can take the international registration down with it. The Hague System does something comparable for industrial designs.

Questions the treaties leave open include exhaustion, the rule on whether the owner's rights end after the first authorised sale. TRIPS Article 6 leaves members free to choose between national, regional and international exhaustion. In Kirtsaeng v. Wiley (US 2013), the Supreme Court held that the first-sale doctrine applies to copies of copyrighted works lawfully made abroad, so a buyer may resell them in the United States without the copyright owner's permission. Newer treaties include the Marrakesh Treaty of 2013 on access to works for people with print disabilities and, as of this writing, a 2024 WIPO treaty on genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge that has not yet entered into force and would require patent applicants to disclose the origin of genetic resources.

Worked example. A Japanese inventor files in Japan on 1 March, then within 12 months files a PCT application claiming priority, and later enters the national phase in the United States and Germany at about 30 months from 1 March. The priority date protects against intervening disclosures in all three. Germany may grant the patent while the United States refuses it, because each office applies its own law.

lessons.title: Structuring a Cross-Border Deal: Law, Forum, Payment and Enforcement
body: A cross-border contract is only as good as the ability to enforce it, so the best drafters work backward from enforcement. Where will the counterparty's assets be, and which forum's decision can reach them? That question drives the choices of law, forum and payment mechanism.

Governing law is generally chosen by the parties. In the EU the Rome I Regulation gives effect to the parties' choice, with limits for consumer and employment contracts and overriding mandatory rules. In the United States, courts follow the Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws section 187 and generally enforce the choice unless the chosen state has no substantial relationship or the application would offend a fundamental policy of a state with a materially greater interest. Parties should also decide whether to exclude the CISG, since a general choice of a contracting state's law leaves it applicable.

Forum comes next, and here the legal landscape is uneven. Court judgments circulate far less easily than arbitral awards. In The Bremen v. Zapata (US 1972), the Supreme Court held that forum selection clauses in international contracts are presumptively valid and enforced absent fraud, overreaching or a strong public policy against it. Two Hague conventions try to improve cross-border judgment enforcement. The Choice of Court Convention of 2005, in force since 2015 for the EU, Mexico, Singapore and some other states, requires parties to respect exclusive choice-of-court agreements and recognise resulting judgments. The Judgments Convention of 2019, in force since September 2023 for the EU and Ukraine, and later for others including the United Kingdom, provides common grounds for recognition of foreign civil and commercial judgments. As of this writing the United States has signed but not ratified either, so a US judgment may need to be enforced under the local law of the country where assets are found. By contrast, the New York Convention provides worldwide enforcement of arbitral awards, which is why arbitration is the usual choice where the counterparty's assets are in countries without strong judgment treaties. A well-drafted clause names the rules or institution, the seat, the number of arbitrators, the language and the governing law, and avoids vague or pathological wording that invites a challenge.

If the counterparty is a state or a state-owned enterprise, sovereign immunity matters. In the United States, the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act of 1976 gives foreign states immunity with exceptions, including for commercial activity and for agreements to arbitrate. Execution against state property has narrower exceptions than jurisdiction.

Payment security protects the seller. In a documentary letter of credit governed by the ICC's Uniform Customs and Practice for Documentary Credits (UCP 600), a bank undertakes to pay against conforming documents. The credit is independent of the underlying sale (the autonomy principle), so the bank examines documents, not performance, and strict compliance is required. Courts allow an exception for fraud, but only in narrow cases. Other tools include advance payment, bank guarantees and standby credits, trade credit insurance and escrow.

Worked example. A Dutch exporter sells equipment to a buyer in a country with no judgments treaty with the Netherlands, and the buyer's assets are in that country. The exporter should choose ICC arbitration with a neutral seat in a New York Convention state, require a confirmed letter of credit, and decide whether to exclude the CISG.

lessons.title: Analysing a Cross-Border Deal: A Worked Method
body: A cross-border deal touches many bodies of law at once, and the practical skill is sequencing. A reliable method is to ask a fixed set of questions in an order that puts legality before drafting. First, identify the parties, their places of business and ownership, and what is being exchanged: goods, services, intellectual property, data, or an equity stake. This fact base determines which regimes apply.

Second, run the gating issues, which decide whether the deal can happen at all. Screen every party and its owners against sanctions lists and apply the 50 percent rule. Classify the product and technology for export control purposes and check whether a licence is needed, including for re-exports and for end users. Check whether the buyer's government or a state-owned entity is involved, which raises anti-corruption and sovereign immunity questions. If an acquisition is involved, consider foreign investment screening in the target's country. If personal data will move across borders, identify the transfer mechanism. Failure at this stage can make the contract unenforceable or expose the parties to penalties regardless of the deal terms.

Third, address the trade-law layer. Classify the goods under the Harmonized System, work out valuation and origin, identify the applicable duties and any preferential agreement and its rules of origin, and check for trade remedies or technical and health rules that apply to the product.

Fourth, set the contract framework. Decide whether the CISG applies to a sale of goods, and whether to exclude it. Choose governing law, an Incoterm that allocates delivery, cost and risk, and a payment mechanism. Allocate risk through warranties, limitation of liability, force majeure and termination rights, while remembering that some rules, such as sanctions and anti-corruption laws, cannot be contracted away. Draft sanctions and compliance clauses, including rights to suspend for legal risk.

Fifth, plan disputes and enforcement: arbitration with a seat in a New York Convention state, or courts where a judgments treaty applies, and, for large investments, whether a treaty-based route exists, remembering the abuse-of-process limit on restructuring after a dispute is foreseeable.

Worked example. A US machine tool maker agrees to sell 40 precision machines to a distributor in Country K, to be resold to a manufacturer there. The first pass shows that the goods are classified under an ECCN requiring a licence for K, that the distributor is 55 percent owned by a company on the SDN list, and that the distributor proposes to pay a large commission to an unnamed local consultant. The deal cannot proceed as proposed. The sanctions problem alone blocks dealing with the distributor, and the commission raises FCPA exposure through a possible red flag. If those problems were cured, for example by selling to a different, screened distributor and licensing the export, the CISG would apply by default since both states are parties unless excluded, the parties could choose CIF with a confirmed letter of credit, and an ICC arbitration clause with a neutral seat would let the seller enforce an award where the buyer's assets lie. The lesson is that legality gates come first, and drafting comes second.

questions.prompt: Under GATT Article II, what does a tariff binding commit a member to?
choices: Reducing every bound rate each year by a percentage that the Ministerial Conference decides
Eliminating tariffs on all goods that are produced by another member within five years of joining
Not applying a tariff on a bound product above the maximum rate listed in its schedule of concessions
Applying exactly the rate in its schedule to products from all members, so a lower applied rate would breach the binding

questions.prompt: Which GATT rule most directly addresses an internal tax that falls more heavily on imported goods than on like domestic goods?
choices: Article I, which requires a member to give the like product of every other member the best treatment it grants any member
Article XI, which prohibits quotas and other quantitative import restrictions at the border
Article II, which sets the ceiling on the tariffs a member may impose on a listed product
Article III, which requires national treatment for imported products once they have entered the market

questions.prompt: Country A applies a 5 percent tariff to bicycles from Country B, a WTO member, and 9 percent to like bicycles from Country C, also a member, with no trade agreement involved. What is the best analysis?
choices: A breach of Article I, since the lower rate must be extended to like bicycles from all members
Consistent with GATT, because both rates fall below the bound rate in Country A's schedule
A breach of Article XI, because the differential operates in practice as a quantitative restriction
Consistent with GATT, since tariff levels are a sovereign matter that remains open to discrimination

questions.prompt: Country D imposes an excise tax on imported spirits at a rate double the rate on domestic spirits made from different raw materials, which consumers treat as direct substitutes. D argues the products are not like and no Article III breach exists. Which line of reasoning best tests D's position?
choices: Whether D is a developing country, because the Enabling Clause suspends national treatment for those members
Whether the products are at least directly competitive or substitutable, which brings the second sentence of Article III:2 into play
Whether the tax exceeds the bound rate for spirits in D's schedule, since Article II governs charges on imported goods including internal taxes
Whether the tax is applied at the border, because any measure imposed on importation falls outside Article III entirely

questions.prompt: Country E prohibits imports of a product from Country F, with which it has no FTA, but allows it from all other members, citing a political dispute. F, a member, challenges. Which claim has the strongest basis?
choices: Article III alone, since only measures that affect internal sale of products can be challenged before a panel
Article XXIV, since the measure undermines the customs union that E has formed with the other members
Article XI:1 for the quantitative ban and Article I for the discrimination against F's product alongside other members' goods
Article II, since a ban operates as a tariff of infinite height that exceeds the bound rate set out in E's schedule for the product

questions.prompt: Under GATS, which mode of supply describes a foreign bank establishing a subsidiary in the host country?
choices: Mode 4, presence of natural persons who supply the service
Mode 3, commercial presence in the territory of the member
Mode 1, cross-border supply of the service from abroad
Mode 2, consumption of the service by a person abroad

questions.prompt: Why can Country X restrict foreign suppliers in a service sector it did not list in its GATS schedule, without breaching market access or national treatment?
choices: Articles XVI and XVII bind a member only in sectors and modes it has scheduled, under the positive list approach
GATS contains no market access or national treatment rules and relies solely on MFN treatment in Article II
Services trade is wholly outside the WTO system unless the supplier is a natural person under Mode 4
Unscheduled sectors fall under a general exception allowing any measure the member regards as necessary for its economy

questions.prompt: What does Article 31bis of TRIPS, in force since 2017, accomplish?
choices: It extends the minimum patent term for pharmaceuticals beyond 20 years for members that are developing countries
It bars compulsory licensing of any medicine in a member that has an active national public health emergency
It exempts all vaccine patents from enforcement during pandemics declared by the World Health Organization
It lets a country export medicines made under compulsory licence to members lacking manufacturing capacity

questions.prompt: Country M has scheduled national treatment for telecommunications Mode 3 with the limitation that foreign ownership cannot exceed 49 percent. It then enacts a rule requiring foreign operators to be wholly domestic-owned. What is the best analysis?
choices: Consistent with GATS, because Mode 3 commitments are outside the scope of the agreement's market access rules
A breach of TRIPS Article 3, since foreign-owned operators hold national treatment for their intellectual property
A likely breach of GATS Article XVII or XVI, because the new rule goes beyond the limitation M entered in its schedule
Consistent with GATS, because a member may always tighten a restriction after scheduling a sector for national treatment

questions.prompt: Country N, a TRIPS member, grants patents for all inventions except drug products, which it treats as unpatentable, and offers a 10-year term for the rest. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: N is in compliance if its patent policy is intended to improve public access to medicines for its population
N is likely in breach of Article 27.1 on fields of technology and of the minimum 20-year term in Article 33
N is in compliance, since TRIPS leaves each member free to set the scope and term of patent protection
N is in breach only of Article 4 on most-favoured-nation treatment, since TRIPS sets no substantive patent standards

questions.prompt: What does the negative (reverse) consensus rule mean for establishing a WTO panel?
choices: A panel is set up at the second request unless all members, including the complainant, agree not to
A panel is set up only when the Dispute Settlement Body reaches positive consensus, with the respondent able to block it
A panel is set up once the Director-General has conciliated for 60 days without success
A panel is set up when a simple majority of members votes to approve the complainant's request

questions.prompt: Why can a losing party stop a panel report from becoming binding by appealing it, as of this writing?
choices: The DSU suspends all panel reports during the pendency of any reform negotiations among the membership
Adoption waits for the appeal to conclude, and the Appellate Body lacks the three members needed to hear it
The Appellate Body hears the appeal but has made no final reports since the United States blocked its budget
Panel reports bind only after a vote by the General Council, where the appealing party holds a veto

questions.prompt: What is the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA)?
choices: A mechanism that lets any WTO member impose retaliation without waiting for authorisation by the Dispute Settlement Body
